definition: Automatic taxonomy construction (ATC) is the use of software programs to generate taxonomical classifications from a body of texts called a corpus.
details: ATC is a branch of natural language processing, which in turn is a branch of artificial intelligence. A taxonomy (or taxonomical classification) is a scheme of classification, especially, a hierarchical classification, in which things are organized into groups or types. Among other things, a taxonomy can be used to organize and index knowledge (stored as documents, articles, videos, etc.), such as in the form of a library classification system, or a search engine taxonomy, so that users can more easily find the information they are searching for. Many taxonomies are hierarchies (and thus, have an intrinsic tree structure), but not all are. Manually developing and maintaining a taxonomy is a labor-intensive task requiring significant time and resources, including familiarity of or expertise in the taxonomy's domain (scope, subject, or field), which drives the costs and limits the scope of such projects. Also, domain modelers have their own points of view which inevitably, even if unintentionally, work their way into the taxonomy. ATC uses artificial intelligence techniques to quickly automatically generate a taxonomy for a domain in order to avoid these problems and remove limitations.

explainer.lead: Automatic taxonomy construction uses software to turn a collection of texts into an organized classification scheme. It can make large bodies of knowledge easier to index and search without requiring people to build and maintain every category by hand.

tiers.eli5: Imagine emptying a huge box of mixed-up library cards and having a computer sort them into sensible shelves and sections. Automatic taxonomy construction does something similar with a collection of writings, creating groups—and often smaller groups inside bigger ones—so information is easier to find.
tiers.practitioner: ATC is applied to a domain corpus when manually creating and maintaining a classification would be too costly or narrow. The resulting taxonomy can support document indexing or search, but corpus coverage and the viewpoints embedded in the domain still matter, so expert review remains useful.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a corpus C, automatic taxonomy construction seeks to generate a taxonomical classification T for C's domain, often a tree-structured hierarchy of groups or types. It is a branch of natural language processing and artificial intelligence; its scope and quality depend on the corpus, and automatic construction does not guarantee a complete or unbiased taxonomy.

explainer.example: For a corpus of articles about animals, the software might produce a hierarchy with broad animal groups and narrower groups beneath them. Those categories could then index the articles so a user can browse from a general group to more specific material.

usedIn.name: Library classification
usedIn.detail: Organizes documents and other stored knowledge into categories that help users locate material.

usedIn.name: Search engines
usedIn.detail: Provides a taxonomy for organizing and indexing information so searches are easier to navigate.

usedIn.name: Knowledge indexing
usedIn.detail: Classifies documents, articles, videos, and similar resources within a particular domain.

explainer.intuition: Instead of asking experts to decide every category and relationship in advance, let software infer a classification scheme from the texts themselves. The aim is a useful map of a subject area, often shaped like a tree.
howItWorks: Collect a body of texts, called a corpus, for the domain.
Use software and artificial intelligence techniques to derive groups or types represented in that corpus.
Arrange those groups into a taxonomical classification, commonly a hierarchy.
Use the generated taxonomy to organize and index knowledge for retrieval.
explainer.whyItMatters: Manual taxonomy work demands substantial time, resources, and domain expertise, which raises costs and limits scope. Automation can generate a domain taxonomy quickly and reduce dependence on an individual modeler's point of view, although it does not remove every limitation.
misconceptions: Every taxonomy is a strict hierarchy: many are trees, but not all.
Automatic means no human judgment is involved anywhere: the corpus and domain choices still shape the result.
ATC is the same as search: it builds a classification that can support search, rather than performing the search itself.
